fit_paragraph: Long-term fiscal policy is where my convenience yield paper lands: it measures what a government's issuance does to the price of safety for other sovereigns, which is the cost of public debt in a currency union, and my work with Boris Hofmann on productivity and inflation across 130 years and 17 advanced economies speaks to the long-run growth and inflation conditions under which public debt is sustainable. A fellowship year would let me take both projects to the United States: the convenience yield results outside the euro area, and the historical work to the question of what AI-driven productivity growth would mean for debt dynamics.

position: Two Assistant Professor positions in Economics
fit_paragraph: IESE's economics group sits between my two papers, one on inflation and one on the price of safe debt, and Barcelona's economics community around the BSE is one of the densest in Europe. I would bring to IESE's classrooms the presentation style an internship at BlackRock taught me, which is what its MBA students expect, and the experience of teaching students who work alongside their studies.

position_phrase: a Post-doctoral Fellow in Wealth and Income Inequality
institution_opening: the National Bureau of Economic Research
fit_paragraph: Wealth and income inequality meet my research at the point where macroeconomic shocks hit people unevenly. My job market paper shows that units differ in their exposure to common shocks and develops a two-step design that separates the common from the idiosyncratic component in a panel; applied to household data, the same design measures how an inflation surge or a change in safe asset returns is distributed across the income and wealth distribution. A fellowship year would let me take the design from sectors to households.

Bristol's economics school is a natural home for my research, which is macroeconomics with a finance question beside it: the Phillips curve paper asks how inflation responds to labor shortages when units differ in their exposure to common shocks, and the convenience yield paper how debt issuance in one country moves the price of safety in another. The United Kingdom is where my research took its current shape: I spent 2025--26 at the LSE, and the network of macroeconomists I built there is one I would keep working with from Bristol. I would be glad to teach macroeconomics at every level.

position: Postdoc: Automation and the Labour Market in the Global Economy
position_phrase: a Postdoctoral Researcher on the project ``Automation and the Labour Market in the Global Economy''
fit_paragraph: The project's question, what automation does to labor markets in a global economy, meets my research at the labor market. My job market paper uses firms' own reports of labor shortages across sectors and countries to measure what tightness does to prices, and the tool I develop there, a two-step design that separates common from idiosyncratic shocks, applies to automation as well: a technology that hits all sectors but not equally. I would bring that tool and experience with European survey data to the project, and I would be glad to teach macroeconomics and labor economics in Aarhus.

institution_opening: the Janeway Institute, University of Cambridge
fit_paragraph: The Janeway Institute is a natural place for the next steps of my research. Vasco Carvalho's work on production networks and sectoral shocks is the closest existing framework to the heterogeneous exposure to common shocks my job market paper identifies, and the Institute's macroeconomists are those I would most like to discuss its next step with: taking the two-step design from sectors to firms. The convenience yield paper would find its readers in Cambridge's finance group.

Yale SOM's finance group is where my job market paper would find its closest readers. Gary Gorton's work on safe debt and the demand for safe assets is the question my convenience yield paper measures from the supply side, and Alp Simsek's work on the links between financial markets and the macroeconomy is the frame for both of my papers. I would bring a European complement to the group's work on Treasury markets: the euro area has several safe issuers in one currency, a setting in which spillovers between convenience yields can be measured directly.

position: Postdoc in Climate- and Macroeconometrics (Leverhulme, 5 yrs)
position_phrase: a Postdoctoral Researcher in Climate and Macroeconometrics
fit_paragraph: Climate is the common shock with the most heterogeneous exposure, and that is the problem my job market paper solves. Units that differ in their exposure to a common shock bias the cross-sectional designs used to identify its effect, and the two-step extension of interactive fixed effects I develop separates the common from the idiosyncratic component under testable conditions. I would bring that macroeconometric tool to the project's questions, together with experience with large European sector-by-country panels.

position: Assistant Professor of Finance (incl. international finance)
fit_paragraph: The position's interest in international finance is where my job market paper sits: it measures how debt issuance in one country moves the price of safety in another, and shows that the spillover depends on how safe the receiving issuer is. The Phillips curve paper adds a second international dimension, separating the shocks a country shares with its neighbors from its own. I would be glad to teach international finance and asset pricing at KU, and I would bring to the classroom the presentation style an internship at BlackRock taught me.

DePaul's finance department is a natural home for my research, which is finance with a macroeconomic question at its core: the convenience yield paper measures how debt issuance in one country moves the price of safety in another, and the Phillips curve paper how inflation responds to scarcity in labor markets. Chicago also puts the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago next door for the policy dialogue I value. I would bring to DePaul's classrooms the experience of teaching finance to students who work alongside their studies, and the presentation style an internship at BlackRock taught me.

position_phrase: a Postdoctoral Fellow in the Young Scholars Program
institution_opening: the Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research (SIEPR)
fit_paragraph: SIEPR's Young Scholars Program is where I would most like to spend a postdoctoral year, between Stanford's macroeconomists and its policy audience. Monika Piazzesi's and Luigi Bocola's work on bond markets and sovereign debt is close to my convenience yield paper, and the Phillips curve paper, which separates the response of inflation to local labor shortages from the response to shared ones, speaks directly to the policy debate SIEPR serves. My positions at the BIS and the ESM taught me how research is used when an institution must act on it.

institution_opening: the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago
fit_paragraph: The Chicago Fed's research department works on both of my questions. Bart Hobijn's work on labor market dynamics and price measurement is close to my job market paper, which asks how inflation responds to labor shortages and shows that the response is about five times larger when shortages are shared across the economy than when they are local, and the convenience yield paper speaks to the financial economics side of the department. My positions at the BIS and the ESM taught me to write for policymakers under deadline.

The EUI is where I would most like to spend my postdoctoral years. Giancarlo Corsetti's work on international macroeconomics and sovereign debt in the euro area is the closest research program to my own, the Department of Economics has the macro group my job market paper needs for its next step, and the Florence School of Banking and Finance keeps the policy dialogue I value within the same institute. The Max Weber Programme's emphasis on teaching and academic practice is also what I need at this stage: I have taught online for three years and want to become a better teacher in the classroom. Returning to Italy for this would be a pleasure.

institution_opening: the University of Chicago Booth School of Business
fit_paragraph: Booth's macro group is where my job market paper would find its closest readers. Elisa Rubbo's work on how macroeconomic shocks reach industries and labor markets is the closest existing research program to the paper's finding that units differ in their exposure to common shocks, and Veronica Guerrieri's and Joseph Vavra's work on business cycles, price setting and monetary policy is the frame for what the paper finds about inflation. The convenience yield paper would find its readers in Booth's finance group.

institution_opening: the University of Chicago Booth School of Business
fit_paragraph: Booth's finance group is where the questions in my research are asked most directly. Stefan Nagel's work on the liquidity premium of near-money assets is the closest existing measurement to the convenience yields my job market paper studies, and Ralph Koijen's demand-based approach to asset pricing is the natural framework for its result that spillovers depend on how close substitutes safe bonds are. I would bring a European complement to the group's work on Treasury markets: the euro area has several safe issuers in one currency, a setting in which spillovers between convenience yields can be measured directly.

institution: University of Chicago, Department of Economics
fit_paragraph: Chicago's macro group is a natural home for my job market paper. Robert Shimer's work on labor market search is the theory behind the tightness the paper measures through firms' reported shortages, and Fernando Alvarez's on price setting and monetary economics is the frame for what the paper finds about inflation. The convenience yield paper would find its readers at Booth. I would be glad to teach macroeconomics at every level.
